documents.text:
Machine Learning
Basic Algorithms
Concept  ·  Worked example  ·  Working code

P A R T O N E
Supervised learning
Learns from labeled input–output pairs. You give it the right answers, it learns the mapping.

1
Linear regression
Fits a straight line to predict a continuous number.
H O W I T W O R K S
•
Finds the line score = m x hours + b that sits closest to all 
points.
•
"Closest" = smallest sum of squared vertical gaps (residuals).
•
Squaring punishes big misses more than small ones.
•
Use it when the output is a number: price, score, 
temperature.
E X A M P L E
Hours studied to exam score
1 hr  ->  50        4 hrs  ->  70
2 hrs ->  55        5 hrs  ->  85
3 hrs ->  65
Learned line:  score = 8.5 x hours + 42
Predict 6 hrs  ->  93
Linear regression  ·  concept

1
Linear regression — code
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
# dataset: hours studied -> exam score
X = np.array([[1], [2], [3], [4], [5]])     # 2D: rows = samples
y = np.array([50, 55, 65, 70, 85])          # 1D: one target each
model = LinearRegression()
model.fit(X, y)                             # learns m and b
print(model.coef_[0], model.intercept_)     # 8.5 , 42
print(model.predict([[6]]))                 # -> 93
xs = np.linspace(0.5, 6.5, 100).reshape(-1, 1)
plt.scatter(X, y, color='tomato')           # the data
plt.plot(xs, model.predict(xs), color='steelblue')   # the line
plt.show()
Key idea: .fit() finds the best line, .predict() uses it. reshape(-1,1) makes the 2D shape sklearn needs.

2
Logistic regression
Despite the name, this is classification — it predicts a class, not a number.
H O W I T W O R K S
•
Pushes a linear score through a sigmoid to get a probability 
0–1.
•
Applies a threshold (usually 0.5) to pick the class.
•
Output is an S-curve, not a straight line.
•
Use it for yes/no questions: pass/fail, spam/not spam, 
churn/stay.
E X A M P L E
Will the student pass?
1.5 hrs  ->  P(pass) = 0.08  ->  FAIL
3.5 hrs  ->  P(pass) = 0.52  ->  PASS
5.0 hrs  ->  P(pass) = 0.91  ->  PASS
Threshold at 0.5 splits the two classes.
Logistic regression  ·  concept

2
Logistic regression — code
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
# dataset: hours studied -> 0 = fail, 1 = pass
X = np.array([[1], [1.5], [2], [3], [4], [5], [5.5]])
y = np.array([0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1])         # categorical target
model = LogisticRegression()
model.fit(X, y)
for hrs in [1.5, 3.5, 5]:
    p = model.predict_proba([[hrs]])[0][1]  # col 1 = P(pass)
    print(hrs, round(p, 2), 'PASS' if p > 0.5 else 'FAIL')
xs = np.linspace(0, 7, 300).reshape(-1, 1)
plt.plot(xs, model.predict_proba(xs)[:, 1])  # the S-curve
plt.axhline(0.5, ls='--', color='gray')      # threshold
plt.show()
predict_proba gives probabilities; predict gives the hard label. Column 1 is the positive class.

3
Decision tree
A flowchart of yes/no questions you can read top to bottom.
H O W I T W O R K S
•
At each step picks the question that best separates the 
classes.
•
"Best" is measured by Gini impurity or information gain.
•
Fully interpretable — you can explain every decision.
•
Limit depth, or it memorises the training data (overfitting).
E X A M P L E
Loan approval
Income > $50k ?
   No   ->  REJECT
   Yes  ->  Credit score > 700 ?
               No   ->  REJECT
               Yes  ->  APPROVE
Applicant: $75k, score 780  ->  APPROVE
Decision tree  ·  concept

3
Decision tree — code
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, plot_tree
# dataset: [income_k, credit_score] -> 1 = approve
X = [[30, 650], [40, 720], [45, 690], [60, 750], [70, 800],
     [55, 640], [80, 710], [35, 800], [90, 660], [65, 730]]
y = [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1]
model = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=2, random_state=0)
model.fit(X, y)                # max_depth stops overfitting
print(model.predict([[75, 780]]))          # -> [1] APPROVE
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plot_tree(model, feature_names=['income_k', 'credit_score'],
          class_names=['Reject', 'Approve'], filled=True)
plt.show()
plot_tree draws the actual learned tree — the clearest algorithm to show students, because the logic is visible.

4
K-nearest neighbours
No training at all — it just remembers the data and votes.
H O W I T W O R K S
•
Stores every training point; does the work at prediction time.
•
For a new point, finds the k closest points by distance.
•
Takes a majority vote among those k neighbours.
•
k is the one parameter to tune: small k = noisy, large k = 
blurry.
E X A M P L E
Apple or orange?
Features: weight, redness
New fruit:  [2.7, 1.5]
3 nearest neighbours:
   apple, apple, apple
Vote  ->  APPLE
K-nearest neighbours  ·  concept

4
K-nearest neighbours — code
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
# dataset: [weight, redness]
X = np.array([[1.8, 1.2], [2.2, 1.6], [2.6, 1.0], [1.5, 1.8],
              [4.0, 2.5], [4.5, 2.2], [4.8, 2.7], [4.2, 2.0]])
y = np.array(['apple'] * 4 + ['orange'] * 4)   # string labels are fine
model = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=3)    # k = 3
model.fit(X, y)                # just stores the data
new = np.array([[2.7, 1.5]])
print(model.predict(new))                      # -> ['apple']
dist, idx = model.kneighbors(new)   # who voted, and how far
print([y[i] for i in idx[0]])       # the 3 neighbour labels
KNN's .fit() does no learning — all computation happens at predict time. That makes it slow on big datasets.

5
Support vector machine
Draws the boundary with the widest possible gap between classes.
H O W I T W O R K S
•
Finds the separating line that maximises the margin.
•
Only the closest points — the support vectors — define it.
•
All other training points could be deleted without changing it.
•
The kernel trick bends the boundary for non-separable data.
E X A M P L E
Spam vs business email
Features: spammy words, business words
Spam:  [5,0]  [6,1]  [4,0]  [7,1]
Ham:   [0,5]  [1,6]  [0,4]  [1,7]
Boundary sits exactly midway,
held in place by the support vectors.
Support vector machine  ·  concept

5
Support vector machine — code
from sklearn.svm import SVC
# dataset: [spammy_words, business_words] -> 1 = spam
X = np.array([[5, 0], [6, 1], [4, 0], [7, 1],
              [0, 5], [1, 6], [0, 4], [1, 7]])
y = np.array([1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0])
model = SVC(kernel='linear')   # 'rbf' curves the boundary
model.fit(X, y)
print(model.support_vectors_)  # the points that define it
xx, yy = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-1, 8, 200),
                     np.linspace(-1, 8, 200))
Z = model.decision_function(np.c_[xx.ravel(), yy.ravel()])
plt.contour(xx, yy, Z.reshape(xx.shape), levels=[-1, 0, 1])
plt.show()                     # boundary + both margins
The meshgrid + decision_function + contour pattern draws ANY 2D decision boundary — reuse it for other classifiers.

6
Naive Bayes
Multiplies word probabilities together using Bayes' theorem.
H O W I T W O R K S
•
Learns P(word | spam) for every word from training data.
•
Multiplies them to score a new message.
•
"Naive" = assumes words are independent of each other.
•
That assumption is false, yet it works very well on text.
E X A M P L E
Spam detection
P('free'   | spam) = 0.8
P('winner' | spam) = 0.9
P('click'  | spam) = 0.6
Email: "free winner click"
Combined  ->  classified SPAM
Naive Bayes  ·  concept

6
Naive Bayes — code
from sklearn.naive_bayes import MultinomialNB
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer
emails = ['free winner click now', 'free money winner',
          'click free prize',      'meeting tomorrow report',
          'project deadline monday', 'lunch meeting notes']
labels = ['spam', 'spam', 'spam', 'ham', 'ham', 'ham']
vec = CountVectorizer()        # text -> word counts
X = vec.fit_transform(emails)  # builds vocab + transforms
model = MultinomialNB()        # NB variant for count data
model.fit(X, labels)
test = vec.transform(['free winner click'])
print(model.predict_proba(test))   # P(ham), P(spam)
print(model.predict(test))         # -> ['spam']
CountVectorizer turns text into numbers first — every text model needs this step. Use transform (not fit_transform) on test data.

P A R T T W O
Unsupervised learning
No labels at all. The algorithm finds structure in the data on its own.

7
K-means clustering
Groups data into k clusters with no labels given.
H O W I T W O R K S
•
Pick k. Place k centroids at random starting positions.
•
Assign every point to its nearest centroid.
•
Move each centroid to the average of its assigned points.
•
Repeat until the centroids stop moving.
E X A M P L E
Customer segments
Features: purchases/month, avg spend
Cluster 0:  low spenders   (2.5, $32)
Cluster 1:  frequent buyers (13.5, $82)
Cluster 2:  big spenders    (4, $312)
Found without being told the segments.
K-means clustering  ·  concept

7
K-means clustering — code
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
# dataset: [purchases/month, avg spend $] - NO labels
X = np.array([[2, 30],  [3, 35],  [2, 25],  [3, 40],
              [12, 80], [14, 90], [13, 75], [15, 85],
              [4, 300], [5, 350], [3, 280], [4, 320]])
model = KMeans(n_clusters=3, random_state=0, n_init=10)
labels = model.fit_predict(X)   # fit + assign in one call
print(labels)                   # cluster id per customer
print(model.cluster_centers_)   # the 3 centroids
plt.scatter(X[:, 0], X[:, 1], c=labels, cmap='Set2')
plt.scatter(*model.cluster_centers_.T, marker='X', s=300)
plt.show()
Note there is no y anywhere — that is what makes it unsupervised. fit_predict trains and assigns in one step.

8
PCA
Squeezes many features into a few, keeping most of the information.
H O W I T W O R K S
•
Finds new axes pointing along the directions of greatest 
variance.
•
Projects the data onto just the top few of those axes.
•
Always scale your features first, or big units dominate.
•
Used to speed up models and to make data visualisable in 2D.
E X A M P L E
House features
5 features per house:
sqft, bedrooms, age, distance, garage
Compressed to 2 components
PC1 keeps 71% of the variance
PC2 keeps 21%   ->  92% total
PCA  ·  concept

8
PCA — code
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
# [sqft, bedrooms, age, dist_to_school, garage]
X = np.array([[1500, 3, 20, 2.0, 1], [2400, 4, 5, 1.5, 2],
              [1100, 2, 35, 3.0, 1], [3000, 5, 2, 0.8, 3],
              [1800, 3, 15, 2.2, 2], [2200, 4, 10, 1.2, 2]])
X = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)   # ALWAYS scale first
pca = PCA(n_components=2)               # 5 features -> 2
X2 = pca.fit_transform(X)
print(pca.explained_variance_ratio_)    # info kept per axis
print(pca.explained_variance_ratio_.sum())
plt.scatter(X2[:, 0], X2[:, 1])
plt.xlabel('PC1'); plt.ylabel('PC2'); plt.show()
Skipping StandardScaler is the classic PCA mistake — sqft in thousands would swamp bedrooms in single digits.

Which one do I use?
Predict a number
Linear regression
Predict a yes/no class
Logistic regression, SVM, Naive Bayes
Need to explain the decision
Decision tree
Small data, no training time
K-nearest neighbours
Working with text
Naive Bayes
No labels — find groups
K-means clustering
Too many features
PCA

P A R T O N E Supervised learning Learns from labeled input–output pairs. You give it the right answers, it learns the mapping.

1 Linear regression Fits a straight line to predict a continuous number. H O W I T W O R K S • Finds the line score = m x hours + b that sits closest to all points. • "Closest" = smallest sum of squared vertical gaps (residuals). • Squaring punishes big misses more than small ones. • Use it when the output is a number: price, score, temperature. E X A M P L E Hours studied to exam score 1 hr -> 50 4 hrs -> 70 2 hrs -> 55 5 hrs -> 85 3 hrs -> 65 Learned line: score = 8.5 x hours + 42 Predict 6 hrs -> 93 Linear regression · concept

1 Linear regression — code import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression # dataset: hours studied -> exam score X = np.array([[1], [2], [3], [4], [5]]) # 2D: rows = samples y = np.array([50, 55, 65, 70, 85]) # 1D: one target each model = LinearRegression() model.fit(X, y) # learns m and b print(model.coef_[0], model.intercept_) # 8.5 , 42 print(model.predict([[6]])) # -> 93 xs = np.linspace(0.5, 6.5, 100).reshape(-1, 1) plt.scatter(X, y, color='tomato') # the data plt.plot(xs, model.predict(xs), color='steelblue') # the line plt.show() Key idea: .fit() finds the best line, .predict() uses it. reshape(-1,1) makes the 2D shape sklearn needs.

2 Logistic regression Despite the name, this is classification — it predicts a class, not a number. H O W I T W O R K S • Pushes a linear score through a sigmoid to get a probability 0–1. • Applies a threshold (usually 0.5) to pick the class. • Output is an S-curve, not a straight line. • Use it for yes/no questions: pass/fail, spam/not spam, churn/stay. E X A M P L E Will the student pass? 1.5 hrs -> P(pass) = 0.08 -> FAIL 3.5 hrs -> P(pass) = 0.52 -> PASS 5.0 hrs -> P(pass) = 0.91 -> PASS Threshold at 0.5 splits the two classes. Logistic regression · concept

2 Logistic regression — code from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression # dataset: hours studied -> 0 = fail, 1 = pass X = np.array([[1], [1.5], [2], [3], [4], [5], [5.5]]) y = np.array([0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1]) # categorical target model = LogisticRegression() model.fit(X, y) for hrs in [1.5, 3.5, 5]: p = model.predict_proba([[hrs]])[0][1] # col 1 = P(pass) print(hrs, round(p, 2), 'PASS' if p > 0.5 else 'FAIL') xs = np.linspace(0, 7, 300).reshape(-1, 1) plt.plot(xs, model.predict_proba(xs)[:, 1]) # the S-curve plt.axhline(0.5, ls='--', color='gray') # threshold plt.show() predict_proba gives probabilities; predict gives the hard label. Column 1 is the positive class.

3 Decision tree A flowchart of yes/no questions you can read top to bottom. H O W I T W O R K S • At each step picks the question that best separates the classes. • "Best" is measured by Gini impurity or information gain. • Fully interpretable — you can explain every decision. • Limit depth, or it memorises the training data (overfitting). E X A M P L E Loan approval Income > $50k ? No -> REJECT Yes -> Credit score > 700 ? No -> REJECT Yes -> APPROVE Applicant: $75k, score 780 -> APPROVE Decision tree · concept

3 Decision tree — code from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, plot_tree # dataset: [income_k, credit_score] -> 1 = approve X = [[30, 650], [40, 720], [45, 690], [60, 750], [70, 800], [55, 640], [80, 710], [35, 800], [90, 660], [65, 730]] y = [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1] model = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=2, random_state=0) model.fit(X, y) # max_depth stops overfitting print(model.predict([[75, 780]])) # -> [1] APPROVE plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6)) plot_tree(model, feature_names=['income_k', 'credit_score'], class_names=['Reject', 'Approve'], filled=True) plt.show() plot_tree draws the actual learned tree — the clearest algorithm to show students, because the logic is visible.

4 K-nearest neighbours No training at all — it just remembers the data and votes. H O W I T W O R K S • Stores every training point; does the work at prediction time. • For a new point, finds the k closest points by distance. • Takes a majority vote among those k neighbours. • k is the one parameter to tune: small k = noisy, large k = blurry. E X A M P L E Apple or orange? Features: weight, redness New fruit: [2.7, 1.5] 3 nearest neighbours: apple, apple, apple Vote -> APPLE K-nearest neighbours · concept

4 K-nearest neighbours — code from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier # dataset: [weight, redness] X = np.array([[1.8, 1.2], [2.2, 1.6], [2.6, 1.0], [1.5, 1.8], [4.0, 2.5], [4.5, 2.2], [4.8, 2.7], [4.2, 2.0]]) y = np.array(['apple'] * 4 + ['orange'] * 4) # string labels are fine model = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=3) # k = 3 model.fit(X, y) # just stores the data new = np.array([[2.7, 1.5]]) print(model.predict(new)) # -> ['apple'] dist, idx = model.kneighbors(new) # who voted, and how far print([y[i] for i in idx[0]]) # the 3 neighbour labels KNN's .fit() does no learning — all computation happens at predict time. That makes it slow on big datasets.

5 Support vector machine Draws the boundary with the widest possible gap between classes. H O W I T W O R K S • Finds the separating line that maximises the margin. • Only the closest points — the support vectors — define it. • All other training points could be deleted without changing it. • The kernel trick bends the boundary for non-separable data. E X A M P L E Spam vs business email Features: spammy words, business words Spam: [5,0] [6,1] [4,0] [7,1] Ham: [0,5] [1,6] [0,4] [1,7] Boundary sits exactly midway, held in place by the support vectors. Support vector machine · concept

5 Support vector machine — code from sklearn.svm import SVC # dataset: [spammy_words, business_words] -> 1 = spam X = np.array([[5, 0], [6, 1], [4, 0], [7, 1], [0, 5], [1, 6], [0, 4], [1, 7]]) y = np.array([1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0]) model = SVC(kernel='linear') # 'rbf' curves the boundary model.fit(X, y) print(model.support_vectors_) # the points that define it xx, yy = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-1, 8, 200), np.linspace(-1, 8, 200)) Z = model.decision_function(np.c_[xx.ravel(), yy.ravel()]) plt.contour(xx, yy, Z.reshape(xx.shape), levels=[-1, 0, 1]) plt.show() # boundary + both margins The meshgrid + decision_function + contour pattern draws ANY 2D decision boundary — reuse it for other classifiers.

6 Naive Bayes Multiplies word probabilities together using Bayes' theorem. H O W I T W O R K S • Learns P(word | spam) for every word from training data. • Multiplies them to score a new message. • "Naive" = assumes words are independent of each other. • That assumption is false, yet it works very well on text. E X A M P L E Spam detection P('free' | spam) = 0.8 P('winner' | spam) = 0.9 P('click' | spam) = 0.6 Email: "free winner click" Combined -> classified SPAM Naive Bayes · concept

6 Naive Bayes — code from sklearn.naive_bayes import MultinomialNB from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer emails = ['free winner click now', 'free money winner', 'click free prize', 'meeting tomorrow report', 'project deadline monday', 'lunch meeting notes'] labels = ['spam', 'spam', 'spam', 'ham', 'ham', 'ham'] vec = CountVectorizer() # text -> word counts X = vec.fit_transform(emails) # builds vocab + transforms model = MultinomialNB() # NB variant for count data model.fit(X, labels) test = vec.transform(['free winner click']) print(model.predict_proba(test)) # P(ham), P(spam) print(model.predict(test)) # -> ['spam'] CountVectorizer turns text into numbers first — every text model needs this step. Use transform (not fit_transform) on test data.
P A R T T W O Unsupervised learning No labels at all. The algorithm finds structure in the data on its own.

7 K-means clustering Groups data into k clusters with no labels given. H O W I T W O R K S • Pick k. Place k centroids at random starting positions. • Assign every point to its nearest centroid. • Move each centroid to the average of its assigned points. • Repeat until the centroids stop moving. E X A M P L E Customer segments Features: purchases/month, avg spend Cluster 0: low spenders (2.5, $32) Cluster 1: frequent buyers (13.5, $82) Cluster 2: big spenders (4, $312) Found without being told the segments. K-means clustering · concept

7 K-means clustering — code from sklearn.cluster import KMeans # dataset: [purchases/month, avg spend $] - NO labels X = np.array([[2, 30], [3, 35], [2, 25], [3, 40], [12, 80], [14, 90], [13, 75], [15, 85], [4, 300], [5, 350], [3, 280], [4, 320]]) model = KMeans(n_clusters=3, random_state=0, n_init=10) labels = model.fit_predict(X) # fit + assign in one call print(labels) # cluster id per customer print(model.cluster_centers_) # the 3 centroids plt.scatter(X[:, 0], X[:, 1], c=labels, cmap='Set2') plt.scatter(*model.cluster_centers_.T, marker='X', s=300) plt.show() Note there is no y anywhere — that is what makes it unsupervised. fit_predict trains and assigns in one step.

8 PCA Squeezes many features into a few, keeping most of the information. H O W I T W O R K S • Finds new axes pointing along the directions of greatest variance. • Projects the data onto just the top few of those axes. • Always scale your features first, or big units dominate. • Used to speed up models and to make data visualisable in 2D. E X A M P L E House features 5 features per house: sqft, bedrooms, age, distance, garage Compressed to 2 components PC1 keeps 71% of the variance PC2 keeps 21% -> 92% total PCA · concept

8 PCA — code from sklearn.decomposition import PCA from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler # [sqft, bedrooms, age, dist_to_school, garage] X = np.array([[1500, 3, 20, 2.0, 1], [2400, 4, 5, 1.5, 2], [1100, 2, 35, 3.0, 1], [3000, 5, 2, 0.8, 3], [1800, 3, 15, 2.2, 2], [2200, 4, 10, 1.2, 2]]) X = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X) # ALWAYS scale first pca = PCA(n_components=2) # 5 features -> 2 X2 = pca.fit_transform(X) print(pca.explained_variance_ratio_) # info kept per axis print(pca.explained_variance_ratio_.sum()) plt.scatter(X2[:, 0], X2[:, 1]) plt.xlabel('PC1'); plt.ylabel('PC2'); plt.show() Skipping StandardScaler is the classic PCA mistake — sqft in thousands would swamp bedrooms in single digits.
